---
title: "From single cells to type-level Gaussians"
---

DeCovarT does not ingest single-cell profiles. It needs, for each labelled
type $j$, a population-level Gaussian
$(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})$ whose precision is sparse.
This chapter is about **lifting** cell-level observations to that object,
and about **checking** that the lift still represents the cells.

## Alignment of type-level Gaussians {#sec-align}

Three strategies, in increasing ambition:

1.  **Affine invariance / convolution** — closed-form means and
    covariances when cells of **one type** are independent Gaussians.
2.  **Optimal transport** — maps and distances when we do not want to
    assume that the empirical cloud is already that Gaussian, including
    discrete (count) OT and Bures / Wasserstein-robust covariance.
3.  **Resampling** — technical bootstrap of cells, and Monte Carlo from
    mechanistic or copula simulators (`scDesign2`, `scMultiSim`).

## Two aggregations that must not be confused {#sec-align-two-sums}

Write $\boldsymbol{x}_{c\cdot j}$ for the expression vector of cell $c$ in
type $j$, and $n_{j}$ for the number of such cells.

**Type-level (population) pseudo-bulk** — the object of this chapter —

$$
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\cdot j}
=
\sum_{c\in C_{j}} w_{c}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{c\cdot j},
\qquad
\sum_{c}w_{c}=1
\ \text{or}\
w_{c}\equiv 1,
$$ {#eq-type-sum}

is a weighted sum **within one type**. If the cells are independent,
means add and covariances add (with $w_{c}^{2}$). This is the
aggregation that estimates $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}$ and
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$.

**Total bulk** — the DeCovarT observation —

$$
\boldsymbol{y}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J} p_{j}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j}^{\mathrm{pop}}
$$ {#eq-total-bulk}

is a convolution **across types**, with simplex weights $\boldsymbol{p}$.
Independence across types gives
$\mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol{y})=\sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$, which
is the article's likelihood. That $p_{j}^{2}$ is **not** the same
calculation as @eq-type-sum.

The first pipeline described “sum the cells, $\Sigma$ scales by $n$,
zeros of $\Theta$ are preserved” as if it applied to whatever one
calls a pseudo-bulk. The improved pipeline corrected the algebra but
still risked being read as a statement about **total** bulk $\boldsymbol{y}$.
Here we only aggregate **within** type. Convolution across types is
DeCovarT's problem, not the GRN's.

::: {#nte-not-y .callout-important}
## :information_source: We align cells to type-level laws, not to $\boldsymbol{y}$

Alignment, Wasserstein distances, and bootstrap in this chapter compare

$$
\{\boldsymbol{x}_{c\cdot j}\}_{c\in C_{j}}
\quad\text{with}\quad
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}).
$$

They do **not** transport single cells onto a mixed bulk, and they do
not estimate $\boldsymbol{p}$. DecOT (@sec-align-decot) is a bulk
**deconvolution** method that uses Wasserstein loss against a reference;
that is a sibling of DeCovarT, not a way to build $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$.
:::

## Affine lift and the precision-sparsity caveat {#sec-align-invariance}

### Independent Gaussian cells

Assume, for a fixed type $j$ (subscript dropped),

$$
\boldsymbol{x}_{c}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{c},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c})
\quad\text{independent in }c.
$$ {#eq-cell-gauss}

Affine closure of multivariate Gaussians
([linear transformation theorem](https://statproofbook.github.io/P/mvn-ltt.html))
gives

$$
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}
=
\sum_{c} w_{c}\boldsymbol{x}_{c}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}\!\left(
\sum_{c}w_{c}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{c},\;
\sum_{c}w_{c}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}
\right).
$$ {#eq-affine}

Special cases used in practice:

| Weights | Mean | Covariance | Precision |
|---------|------|------------|-----------|
| $w_{c}=1$ (sum of $n$ i.i.d. cells) | $n\boldsymbol{\mu}$ | $n\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ | $n^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ |
| $w_{c}=1/n$ (average) | $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ | $n^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ | $n\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ |
| $w_{c}=S_{c}/\sum S_{c'}$ (library-size weights) | $\sum w_{c}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{c}$ | $\sum w_{c}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}$ | inverse of that sum |

The first pipeline stated that summing or averaging **preserves the
zero pattern of $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$**. That is true **only in the
proportional-covariance case**.

If $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ for all $c$, then
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}}=(\sum_{c}w_{c}^{2})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$
and

$$
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}}
=
\frac{1}{\sum_{c}w_{c}^{2}}\,\boldsymbol{\Theta},
$$ {#eq-theta-scale}

so zeros are exactly preserved. If the cells have genuinely different
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}$,

$$
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}}
=
\Bigl(\sum_{c}w_{c}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}\Bigr)^{-1},
$$ {#eq-theta-sum}

and **inversion does not commute with summation**. There is no general
reason for the zero pattern of $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}}$
to equal any individual cell's precision, or the precision of the
“typical” cell. Heterogeneous cells within a labelled type — a
gastruloid “type” is already a continuum — therefore **break** naïve
sparsity transfer.

**What we do in the core.** Treat labelled cells of type $j$ as
**exchangeable draws from one**
$\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})$, estimate that
law (GGM or PLN), and export it. The affine formulae then describe how
a **pseudo-bulk of i.i.d. draws** from the same law would behave. They
are **not** a licence to average heterogeneous $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}$
and keep the glasso zeros. If `GmGM` (@sec-gmgm) finds a non-trivial
cell-axis precision, the i.i.d. hypothesis is already false and
@eq-theta-scale is an approximation.

### Mean and covariance that DeCovarT actually wants

DeCovarT's $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}$ is a **cross-cell mean** of the
purified profile, analogous to MuSiC's cross-sample mean
[@wangBulkTissueCell2019], not a single latent draw. Empirically,

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}
=
\frac{1}{n_{j}}\sum_{c\in C_{j}}\boldsymbol{x}_{c\cdot j}
\quad\text{(linear scale)},
$$ {#eq-mu-hat}

and $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}$ comes from the GGM / PLN fit on
the gene panel, **not** from the unstructured sample covariance of
thousands of genes (that matrix is singular for $G>n_{j}$ and dense).
The glasso / PLN precision is inverted (or solved) to an SPD covariance
for the likelihood. Scale conventions ($n_{j}$ versus $1$) must be
fixed once: the convolution uses $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$ of the
**population profile**, the same object whose mean is
$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}$, not the covariance of the cell-average
estimator.

## Optimal transport {#sec-align-ot}

OT enters in three mathematically distinct roles. Only the second is
central for exporting $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$.

### Discrete OT between count histograms (DecOT) {#sec-align-decot}

Kantorovich OT between discrete measures $\mu,\nu$ with ground cost
$M$ minimises $\langle M,T\rangle$ over couplings with those
marginals. Entropic regularisation $W_{\gamma}$ makes the problem
strongly convex and solvable by Sinkhorn
(`cours_spatial_omics.qmd`; Cuturi 2013).

**DecOT** [@liuDecotBulkDeconvolutionOptimal2022] uses that loss for
**bulk deconvolution**: cell-type reference histograms $C$ (averaged
scRNA-seq) mix as $CP\approx Y$, and $P$ is estimated by minimising
$\sum_{m}W_{\gamma}(Y_{m},CP_{\cdot m})_{M}$ with an entropic
non-negativity regulariser. The ground cost $M$ encodes **gene–gene**
geometry (co-expression distances), so the loss is not elementwise
$\ell_{2}$ / KL. An ensemble over donor-specific references follows
SCDC.

**What survives under our constraints.** DecOT is a competitor to
DeCovarT's **proportion** step, not a way to estimate
$\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$. Useful ideas to steal:

-   a ground cost on genes can be the same metric that a GGM already
    implies (e.g. $M_{gg'}=1-|\hat\rho_{gg'}|$ on partial
    correlations) — but then OT and the GGM are no longer independent
    evidence;
-   entropic discrete OT is the right language if we align **two count
    histograms** (empirical mean cell versus type-level expected counts
    under PLN);
-   ensemble over donors does not apply (one resource).

Discrete OT on **cells** (transporting $n_{j}$ cells onto $n_{\ell}$
cells of another type) is a **type-matching** problem, not population
GGM estimation. Semi-discrete OT (continuous source, discrete
Laguerre / power cells; `cours_spatial_omics.qmd`) is the natural model
when one side is a fitted Gaussian and the other is a finite cell cloud:
the dual weights $\boldsymbol{\varphi}$ inflate Voronoi cells until masses
match. That is a diagnostic of **which cells** are surprising under
$\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})$, not an
estimator of $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$.

### Gaussian (Bures) Wasserstein — the right metric on DeCovarT objects

For two non-degenerate Gaussians
$P_{0}=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{m}_{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})$ and
$P_{1}=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{m}_{1},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1})$, the
squared 2-Wasserstein distance with quadratic cost splits as

$$
W_{2}^{2}(P_{0},P_{1})
=
\|\boldsymbol{m}_{0}-\boldsymbol{m}_{1}\|_{2}^{2}
+
\operatorname{tr}\Bigl(
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}
-2
\bigl(
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{1/2}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{1/2}
\bigr)^{1/2}
\Bigr).
$$ {#eq-bures}

The second term is the **Bures–Wasserstein** metric on SPD covariances.
The Monge map is affine (Brenier):

$$
T(\boldsymbol{x})
=
\boldsymbol{m}_{1}
+
A(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{m}_{0}),
\qquad
A
=
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2}
\bigl(
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2}
\bigr)^{-1/2}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2},
$$ {#eq-monge-gauss}

when the covariances are invertible. **No discrete cell-to-cell OT is
required** merely to transport one fitted type-level Gaussian into
another, or to transport a Gaussian approximation of the cell cloud
onto the exported $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})$.

Entropic OT between Gaussians remains closed form
[@janatiEntropicOptimalTransport2020] and stays well behaved for
degenerate covariances — relevant when $G>n_{j}$ before a GGM
projection.

**Core use.** $W_{2}$ between (i) the empirical Gaussian of cells of
type $j$ (or a shrinkage covariance) and (ii) the exported GGM /
PLN Gaussian is the **alignment score** of @sec-metrics-stat. Large
Bures discrepancy with small mean discrepancy means the graph changed
the covariance geometry; the opposite means we only moved the centroid.

### Wasserstein-robust inverse covariance

Nguyen, Kuhn and Mohajerin Esfahani
[@nguyenDistributionallyRobustInverse2018] estimate a precision by
minimising a **worst-case Stein loss** over normal laws within a
Wasserstein ball of the empirical normal $\mathcal{N}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})$.
Without structural constraints the estimator is an analytical
**nonlinear shrinkage** of the sample eigenvalues: invertible for
$G>n$, rotation-equivariant, order-preserving. With
conditional-independence constraints it becomes a sequential quadratic
programme for a GGM.

That is more directly relevant to DeCovarT than OT-as-alignment
theatre: it regularises $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$ **on the SPD manifold
that the likelihood uses**. A composition (improved pipeline;
**proposal**) is

$$
\text{technical type-level covariances}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{Bures / Wasserstein shrinkage or barycentre}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{sparse precision projection}.
$$ {#eq-w2-pipeline}

The barycentre of several bootstrap covariances in Bures geometry is a
principled “average graph-aware covariance” when we do not want to
average precisions (which does not commute with inversion either).

Adversarial alignment notes and `scConfluence` are **not** default
aligners: they target multi-omics / embedding matching, which we
excluded from the core. CARDAMOM-style OT is useful only insofar as the
cost remains quadratic in the same gene space.

## Bootstrap and Monte Carlo {#sec-align-bootstrap}

### Technical bootstrap (available)

Resample cells **with replacement within type**, labels fixed. Each
replicate yields $(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\ast},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}^{\ast})$
and therefore:

-   edge-inclusion frequencies (@sec-metrics-stat);
-   a cloud of SPD covariances whose Bures barycentre is a candidate
    export;
-   Monte Carlo error for MixSim overlap and for DeCovarT $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$
    in downstream simulations.

This is uncertainty **conditional on this gastruloid experiment**. It
does not stand in for organoid-to-organoid variability
[@squairConfrontingFalseDiscoveries2021]. Calling technical
pseudo-bulks “biological replicates” is the error already flagged in
@nte-pseudoreplication.

### Biological bootstrap (unavailable)

Multiple donors or organoids would allow resampling **experimental
units**. Suppinger does not. External cohorts (e.g. GSE250136) are for
**validation**, not for pooling into one $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$ without
a batch model.

### Monte Carlo from generative models {#sec-align-mc}

When we need more type-level profiles than $n_{j}$ cells, or a known
skeleton for BEELINE-style AUPRC, we simulate.

**`scDesign2`** [@sunScDesign2TransparentSimulator2021] fits, per cell
type, a copula: a count marginal (Poisson, NB, ZIP, or ZINB, chosen
per gene) plus a Gaussian copula for dependence (@thm-sklar). It
preserves genes, captures correlations, and can vary cell number and
depth. It is transparent (parameters are means, dispersions, copula
correlations). For our purpose: fit the copula **on the GGM / PLN
skeleton** (constrain or initialise the copula correlation from
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}$), draw synthetic cells, re-aggregate, and
measure how well $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$ is recovered. Using ZINB
marginals should be a sensitivity, not the default, for the same reason
as @nte-drop-zico.

::: {#thm-sklar}
## Sklar's theorem

Let $F$ be a $G$-dimensional cdf with margins $F_{1},\ldots,F_{G}$.
There exists a copula $C:[0,1]^{G}\to[0,1]$ such that

$$
F(x_{1},\ldots,x_{G})
=
C\bigl(F_{1}(x_{1}),\ldots,F_{G}(x_{G})\bigr).
$$ {#eq-sklar}

If every $F_{g}$ is continuous, $C$ is unique. If some margins are
discrete, $C$ is uniquely determined only on
$\operatorname{ran}(F_{1})\times\cdots\times\operatorname{ran}(F_{G})$,
the Cartesian product of the ranges of the marginal cdfs
([Wikipedia: Sklar's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copula_(statistics)#Sklar's_theorem)).
:::

::: {#nte-discrete-copula .callout-note}
## :information_source: Discrete margins: uniqueness fails, so we jitter

The **Gaussian copula** takes $C_{\Theta}$ to be the cdf of a
$G$-dimensional standard normal with correlation (or precision)
$\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ after applying $\Phi^{-1}$ to each uniform margin.
That is the copula behind both `huge.npn` and scDesign2's default
dependence layer; the empirical copula is the rank analogue
([Wikipedia: empirical copulas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copula_(statistics)#Empirical_copulas)).
Other parametric families (Clayton, Gumbel, $t$) change tail
dependence; they are not required for the core simulator.

UMI counts $y_{ig}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}$ are discrete, so @thm-sklar does
**not** give a unique copula density. Two practical patches (Genest and
Nešlehová, 2007, *ASTIN Bulletin*; **not yet in**
`bibliography/REFERENCES.bib`, to add from Zotero before a review pass):

1.  **Jittering / randomised quantile.** Draw
    $U_{ig}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$ independent of the data and set
    $y_{ig}^{\ast}=y_{ig}+U_{ig}-1$ or $y_{ig}^{\ast}=y_{ig}-U_{ig}$,
    then apply the probability-integral transform to obtain
    approximately $\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$ margins on which a Gaussian
    copula is well defined
    ([lecture notes](https://www.karlin.mff.cuni.cz/~antoch/robust16/prednasky/Nedele/genestNeslehova2.pdf)).
2.  **Mass-spreading copulas** (bilinear / checkered extensions,
    Bernstein polynomial approximations) that spread the probability of
    each integer cell uniformly over a rectangle, without adding
    explicit jitter.

scDesign2 implements the copula on estimated count margins; treat
jittering as the justification that a Gaussian copula on UMI tables is
an approximation, not a uniqueness theorem.
:::

**`scMultiSim`** [@liScMultiSimSimulationSinglecell2025a] is a mechanistic
multi-omics simulator: GRN, chromatin, RNA velocity, spatial location,
cell–cell interaction, technical noise. It can **take a GRN as input**
and emit counts — the right tool for a known-skeleton benchmark in the
spirit of BEELINE / SERGIO / dyngen. Most of its modalities (ATAC,
space, velocity) are **out of the core**. The transcriptomic channel
with a user GRN **is** in scope for metrics (@sec-metrics-topo). Do not
fit scMultiSim's full spatial/CCI stack merely to pad Suppinger.

**What we reject as a default generator.** Black-box GANs; simulators
that do not preserve gene identity; using SERGIO's random GRN as if it
were gastruloid biology. The improved pipeline's suggestion to feed the
sparse GGM into scDesign2 / scMultiSim as a prior is the right
**benchmark** design, not a way to invent biological replicates.

## What we would actually run {#sec-align-recommend}

1.  **Default lift.** Independent-type GGM or PLN $\to$ export
    $(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})$ on the linear scale,
    with sparsity transfer trusted only as
    “one $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$ per type”.
2.  **Alignment diagnostic.** Bures–Wasserstein and KL between that
    Gaussian and a shrinkage covariance of the cells; semi-discrete OT
    only if we need to flag outlier cells.
3.  **Uncertainty.** Technical bootstrap; Bures barycentre as an
    optional export; never labelled as biological replication.
4.  **Simulation arm.** `scDesign2` copula constrained by
    $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}$; `scMultiSim` RNA channel when a
    known skeleton is required for AUPRC.
5.  **Not in the core.** DecOT as a DeCovarT replacement; scConfluence;
    unbalanced / spatial OT; averaging heterogeneous cell-level
    precisions and keeping the zeros.

The first pipeline's affine story is kept as the **i.i.d. special
case**. The improved pipeline's sparsity caveat and Wasserstein-robust
covariance are the parts that were missing. Both are now stated on
**type-level** sums, not on total bulk $\boldsymbol{y}$.
